summary: Defines RADIUS attributes used to configure IPv4-over-IPv6 transition mechanisms based on address plus port, including Lightweight 4over6, MAP-E, and MAP-T. This lets networks that keep subscriber configuration in an AAA server provision these softwire mechanisms centrally.

eli5.summary: When a home connection starts, the provider's guest list can also hand out the special settings needed to use old internet addresses over the new kind of network.

questions: what are the radius softwire46 attributes
subtitle: New RADIUS attributes that let an AAA server hand IPv4-over-IPv6 softwire settings to a broadband gateway.

tldr.problem: Providers moving to IPv6 use A+P softwire mechanisms (MAP-E, MAP-T, Lightweight 4over6) to keep IPv4 working, and DHCPv6 options exist to configure clients. But in many networks the subscriber configuration lives in an AAA server that speaks RADIUS, which had no way to carry these settings.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three extended RADIUS attributes, Softwire46-Configuration (241.9), Softwire46-Priority (241.10) and Softwire46-Multicast (241.11), whose nested fields map one to one onto the DHCPv6 options. The Broadband Network Gateway reads them from the AAA server and uses them to fill in the DHCPv6 options it sends to the customer device.
tldr.outcome: Operators can store softwire configuration centrally in their AAA server and have it flow to customer devices through the existing DHCPv6 exchange, for unicast and multicast alike.

today: RFC 8658 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of these RADIUS attributes for the A+P softwire mechanisms.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Needs Softwire Attributes
sections.content:
Providers are moving to IPv6, and several IPv4 service continuity mechanisms based on Address plus Port (A+P, RFC 6346) carry IPv4 over an IPv6-only network. They are MAP-E (RFC 7597), MAP-T (RFC 7599) and Lightweight 4over6 (RFC 7596). RFC 8114 adds delivery of IPv4 multicast over an IPv6 multicast network. For each of these, DHCPv6 options already exist to configure the client.

In many networks, though, user configuration is kept in an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) server that talks RADIUS. In fixed broadband, the Broadband Network Gateway (BNG) is both a AAA client and the DHCPv6 server for the customer device (the CE). New RADIUS attributes are needed to carry the settings from the AAA server to the BNG so it can pass them on in DHCPv6.

The contents of the new attributes map 1:1 onto the fields of the DHCPv6 options in RFC 7598, RFC 8026 and RFC 8115. The RFC targets deployments where a trusted relationship exists between the RADIUS client and server.
sections.eli5: The provider keeps each customer's settings in one big list. This RFC teaches that list how to pass along the special settings, so the gateway can then hand them to your home router.

sections.title: The Softwire46-Configuration Attribute
sections.content:
The unicast settings travel in Softwire46-Configuration, a tlv-type attribute with Type 241 and Extended-Type 9, written 241.9. Inside it sits one or more of three attributes: Softwire46-MAP-E (TLV-Type 1), Softwire46-MAP-T (2) and Softwire46-Lightweight-4over6 (3). Each may appear at most once, and at least one MUST be present. The BNG SHALL use them to populate the DHCPv6 Softwire46 container options defined in RFC 7598.

Each mechanism requires a different set of sub-attributes. MAP-E needs one rule and at least one border relay address (Softwire46-BR). MAP-T needs one rule and exactly one default mapping rule (Softwire46-DMR). Lightweight 4over6 needs at least one BR and one Softwire46-V4V6Bind. All three MAY carry one Softwire46-PORTPARAMS.

The attribute MAY appear in an Access-Accept, and in an Access-Request to indicate a preferred configuration, though the server need not honor that preference. It MAY also appear in CoA-Request and Accounting-Request packets, and MUST NOT appear in any other RADIUS packet.
sections.eli5: It is a labeled box with a few smaller boxes inside. Which small boxes you must include depends on which kind of translation trick the customer uses.

sections.title: Rules, Relays and Port Sets
sections.content:
Softwire46-Rule comes in two kinds: TLV-Type 4 is the Basic Mapping Rule (not to be used for forwarding) and TLV-Type 5 is a Forwarding Permitted Mapping Rule. Using type 5 is equivalent to setting the F flag in the DHCPv6 OPTION_S46_RULE. A rule holds Rule-IPv6-Prefix (10), Rule-IPv4-Prefix (11) and EA-Length (12), where the Embedded Address length ranges from 0 to 48.

Softwire46-BR (6) is a single IPv6 address of 16 octets for the Border Relay. Softwire46-DMR (7) is an IPv6 prefix, with allowed lengths from 0 to 96. Softwire46-V4V6Bind (8) pairs an IPv4-Address (13), the full or shared IPv4 address of the CE, with a Bind-IPv6-Prefix (14) that tells the CE which prefix to use as the tunnel source.

Softwire46-PORTPARAMS (9) describes how an IPv4 address is shared between clients. It holds PSID-Offset (15), PSID-Len (16) and PSID (17). When PSID-Len is 0 the PSID field is ignored, and the address-sharing ratio is 2^k for a PSID length of k bits. Each of these is encoded in 32 bits, with the value right justified and unused bits set to zero.
sections.eli5: Sharing one street address among many families means each family gets its own set of door numbers. These small pieces say which rule to follow, which relay to use and which door numbers belong to you.

sections.title: Priority and Multicast Attributes
sections.content:
A client may support several mechanisms and request more than one. Softwire46-Priority (241.10) carries an ordered list of Softwire46-Option-Code TLVs (type 18), and the first one listed is the most preferred. It corresponds to OPTION_S46_PRIORITY in RFC 8026. At least one option code MUST be present. The initial codes are 1 for MAP-E, 2 for MAP-T, 3 for Lightweight 4over6 and 144 for DS-Lite.

Softwire46-Multicast (241.11) carries the IPv6 prefixes used to build IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses as in RFC 8114, and the BNG uses them to fill the DHCPv6 PREFIX64 option. It must include ASM-Prefix64 (19) or SSM-Prefix64 (20), or both. Both have to be a /96 prefix in the right multicast range. U-Prefix64 (21) MUST be present when SSM-Prefix64 is, and MAY be present with ASM-Prefix64. Its length MUST be 32, 40, 48, 56, 64 or 96.
sections.eli5: If a home router knows several tricks, the provider can list them in order of favorite. Another box holds the special addresses used for TV-style streams sent to many viewers at once.

sections.title: How RADIUS and DHCPv6 Work Together
sections.content:
The CE sends a DHCPv6 Solicit that asks for a softwire container option: OPTION_S46_CONT_MAPE (94) for MAP-E, OPTION_S46_CONT_MAPT (95) for MAP-T, OPTION_S46_CONT_LW (96) for Lightweight 4over6, or option 113 for multicast. The BNG then sends a RADIUS Access-Request, with a User-Name and User-Password and the matching Softwire46 attribute. If the AAA server authenticates the request and has a suitable configuration, it returns an Access-Accept with the attributes. The BNG maps them into DHCPv6 options, and the CE gets them in the Advertise and Reply messages.

Authorization can be done separately, using an Access-Request with Service-Type 'Authorize Only' (17) and a State attribute. If the BNG gets no softwire attribute back, it may fall back to a preconfigured configuration. If it gets an Access-Reject, it must not supply the configuration to the client.

When configuration changes, such as a new BR address, the AAA server can send a CoA-Request. The BNG then sends a DHCPv6 Reconfigure to the CE, which responds with a Renew or Information-Request to fetch the update. For Lightweight 4over6, the CE binding state must also be synchronized with the lwAFTR/BR, either by static preconfiguration or on demand by the AAA server.
sections.eli5: Your router asks the gateway for its settings. The gateway checks the guest list, gets the answer, and passes it back. If the list changes later, the gateway taps your router on the shoulder to ask it to check again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no security issues inherently different from those in RFC 2865 and, for CoA messages, RFC 5176. The known weaknesses of RADIUS apply, and they impose a requirement to trust the counterparty. For that reason the document targets deployments with a trusted relationship between RADIUS client and server, with communication optionally secured by IPsec or TLS.

The sample process also advises that the Message-Authenticator attribute (type 80) should be used to protect both Access-Request and Access-Accept messages. Security issues of each softwire mechanism, and of the DHCPv6 side between CE and BNG, are left to the RFCs that define them.
sections.eli5: The provider's gateway and its guest list have to trust each other, because the list is only as safe as the link between them. The RFC says to protect that link.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned three attributes from the Short Extended Space of RFC 6929: 241.9 Softwire46-Configuration, 241.10 Softwire46-Priority and 241.11 Softwire46-Multicast, all of data type tlv.

IANA also created a registry called 'RADIUS Softwire46 Configuration and Multicast Attributes', holding the nested values 1 to 21 with 0 reserved and 22-255 unassigned. New entries need Standards Action. A second registry, 'Option Codes Permitted in the Softwire46-Priority Attribute', lists the codes for each mechanism, and new codes can be added through IETF Review.
sections.eli5: The numbers for the new labels were written in the official phone book of RADIUS, so everyone uses the same ones.
